title: Listening practice: A Library Visit, Early Towns, and an Ice Cube Project
description: Three clips to listen to twice: classroom directions, an explanation about early towns, and a student science talk with a claim.

stimuli.title: Listen: Going to the library

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Good morning, class. We are going to the library. First, line up at the door. Bring your reading folder, but leave your lunch box here. In the library, sit on the blue rug and use quiet voices, because other classes are reading too. When I raise my hand, stop talking and look at me, so everyone can hear the next direction. After story time, you may borrow one book.

stimuli.script: Teacher: Good morning, class. We are going to the library. First, line up at the door. Bring your reading folder, but leave your lunch box here. In the library, sit on the blue rug and use quiet voices, because other classes are reading too. When I raise my hand, stop talking and look at me, so everyone can hear the next direction. After story time, you may borrow one book.

stimuli.title: Listen: Early towns

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Many towns in the past began near rivers, and there were good reasons. First, people need fresh water to drink and to wash. A river gave them plenty. Second, the soil near a river is rich, so farmers could grow more food. Third, boats could travel on the river. Because of that, people could carry grain, wood, and cloth to other towns, and they could bring back things they did not have. When a town had water, food, and a way to trade, more families wanted to live there. As a result, the town grew.

stimuli.script: Teacher: Many towns in the past began near rivers, and there were good reasons. First, people need fresh water to drink and to wash. A river gave them plenty. Second, the soil near a river is rich, so farmers could grow more food. Third, boats could travel on the river. Because of that, people could carry grain, wood, and cloth to other towns, and they could bring back things they did not have. When a town had water, food, and a way to trade, more families wanted to live there. As a result, the town grew.

stimuli.title: Listen: Ice cube project

turns.speaker: Lina
turns.text: For my science project, I asked: where does an ice cube melt the fastest? I put one ice cube on a plate in three places. The plate in the sunny window melted in twenty minutes. The plate on the shady shelf melted in thirty-five minutes. The plate in the cool closet took fifty minutes. I think ice melts faster in warmer places, because the sunny window was the warmest spot, and the closet was the coolest.

items.stem: What should students bring to the library?

options.text: Their own lunch box
Their reading folder
A book to take back
The blue rug to sit on

distractors.a: The teacher says to leave the lunch box in the classroom.
distractors.c: The teacher never talks about returning a book. Students borrow one after story time.
distractors.d: The blue rug is where students sit in the library. They do not carry it.

items.explanation: The teacher says, bring your reading folder, but leave your lunch box in the classroom.

support.clue: Listen for the word 'bring' and the word 'but'. They tell you what to take and what to leave.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Pack your swimsuit and a towel, but leave your toys at home.' The word bring points to what you take. The words but leave point to what stays. Listen for both in the library clip.

misconceptions.a: mixes up what to bring and what to leave
misconceptions.c: adds a detail that was not said
misconceptions.d: mixes up a place with a thing to bring

items.stem: Put the teacher's directions in order.
items.explanation: The teacher says first line up at the door, then in the library sit on the blue rug, and after story time borrow one book.

support.clue: Listen for the words 'first', 'in the library', and 'after story time'. They show what to do early and what to do last.
support.frame: First, ______. In the library, ______. After story time, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'First, put on your coat. At the pool, sit on the bench. After the whistle, jump in.' Each direction has its place in time. Put the library directions in order the same way.

items.stem: Why should students use quiet voices in the library?

options.text: Other classes are reading too.
So everyone can hear the next direction.
Students are about to borrow books.
It is time for story time.

distractors.b: The teacher gives this reason for stopping talking when a hand is raised. It is not the reason for quiet voices.
distractors.c: Borrowing a book happens after story time. It is not the reason for quiet voices.
distractors.d: Story time is when students listen, but the teacher gives a different reason for quiet voices.

items.explanation: The teacher says to use quiet voices because other classes are reading too.

support.clue: Listen for the word 'because'. The teacher says the reason right after it.
support.frame: We use quiet voices in the library because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'We wear helmets on bikes because a fall can hurt.' The reason comes after the word because. Listen for the teacher's reason about quiet voices.

misconceptions.b: mixes up two reasons in the talk
misconceptions.c: mixes up what happens later with a reason
misconceptions.d: picks a detail that is near the reason

items.stem: What happened as a result when a town had water, food, and a way to trade?

options.text: Farmers carried soil to other towns.
People left to find a bigger river.
The town grew and became larger.
The river made the soil rich.

distractors.a: The teacher says people carried grain, wood, and cloth, not soil.
distractors.b: The teacher says more families wanted to come, not leave.
distractors.d: Rich soil is one reason the town had food. It is not the result at the end.

items.explanation: The teacher says that when a town had water, food, and a way to trade, more families wanted to live there. As a result, the town grew.

support.clue: Listen for the words 'as a result' at the very end. What happened to the town?
support.model: Mentor example. 'The bakery had fresh bread and a friendly owner. As a result, a long line formed every morning.' The words as a result point to what happened next. Listen for the result in the town talk.

misconceptions.a: mixes up the goods that were traded
misconceptions.d: mixes up a cause with a result

facts: Many early towns grew near rivers, which gave people water, fertile soil, and a way to travel and trade.

items.stem: Match each time word to the river benefit the teacher names.
items.explanation: The teacher names fresh water first, rich soil second, and boats on the river third.

support.clue: Listen for the words 'First', 'Second', and 'Third'. Each one is followed by a river benefit.
support.frame: First, the teacher names ______. Second, ______. Third, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'First, we visited the zoo. Second, we ate lunch. Third, we rode the bus home.' Time words show which thing comes when. Match each time word to the river benefit the teacher names.

facts: Rivers give people fresh water, fertile soil for farming, and a way to travel and move goods by boat.

items.stem: Why could people carry grain, wood, and cloth to other towns?

options.text: People needed fresh water to drink.
The soil near the river was rich.
The towns were close to each other along the water.
Boats could travel on the river.

distractors.a: Fresh water is the first reason in the talk. It does not explain how goods moved.
distractors.b: Rich soil helped farmers grow food. It does not explain how goods moved.
distractors.c: The teacher never says how close the towns were. The reason she gives is how goods could travel.

items.explanation: The teacher says that boats could travel on the river, and because of that, people could carry goods to other towns.

support.clue: Listen for the words 'Because of that'. Listen to what comes just before them.
support.frame: People could carry goods to other towns because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'The new road was smooth, so trucks could drive faster.' The sentence joins one fact to what it made possible. Find the fact that made carrying goods possible in the town talk.

misconceptions.a: picks a different reason from the talk
misconceptions.b: picks a different reason from the talk
misconceptions.c: adds a detail that was not said

facts: Rivers let people travel by boat and carry goods to other towns.

items.stem: How much longer did the ice take to melt in the closet than in the sunny window?

options.text: Fifteen minutes
Thirty minutes
Thirty-five minutes
Fifty minutes

distractors.a: Fifteen is the difference between the shady shelf and the closet, not the window and the closet.
distractors.c: Thirty-five is how long the ice took on the shady shelf.
distractors.d: Fifty is the closet's whole time. The question asks how much longer than the window.

items.explanation: The closet took fifty minutes and the sunny window took twenty minutes, so the closet took thirty minutes longer.

support.clue: Write down the minutes for the sunny window and for the closet. The words 'how much longer' ask you to compare them.
support.frame: The closet took ______ minutes and the window took ______ minutes, so the difference is ______ minutes.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Dev read for forty minutes on Monday and for twenty-five minutes on Tuesday. He read fifteen minutes longer on Monday.' Find the difference between two times the same way.

misconceptions.c: reports one number instead of a difference
misconceptions.d: reports one number instead of a difference

items.stem: Lina says ice melts faster in warmer places. Which fact from her test supports this claim?

options.text: The window ice melted in twenty minutes, but the shelf ice took thirty-five.
The shelf ice melted in twenty minutes, but the window ice took thirty-five.
She put one ice cube on each plate and timed each one.
She tested the ice in three different places in the room.

distractors.b: The places are reversed. The sunny window ice melted in twenty minutes, not the shady shelf ice.
distractors.c: One ice cube on each plate makes a fair test, but it does not show that warmth matters.
distractors.d: Testing different places gives data, but it does not show which place melted ice fastest.

items.explanation: Lina's claim is that warmer places melt ice faster. The sunny window was the warmest spot, and its ice melted in the least time, twenty minutes.

support.clue: Listen for Lina's claim: she says what she thinks. Then listen for the minutes at each place.
support.frame: The claim is supported because the ______ place ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'Kai thinks the tall plant grew more because it got more light. His evidence: the plant by the window grew five centimeters, and the plant in the shade grew two.' Evidence is a result that matches the claim. Listen for Lina's result.

misconceptions.c: uses a fact about the method, not the result
misconceptions.d: uses a fact about the method, not the result

facts: Ice melts faster in warmer places.
